query: For multicomponent high-entropy alloys in solid and liquid states at and near their high melting temperatures, what single testable methodological intervention could overcome the inability of EAM references to represent the many atomic configurations of the ab initio liquid? Explain why it should improve reference–target phase-space overlap, predict the reduction in thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD’s EAM references, define the applicable composition and temperature ranges, identify supporting evidence from elemental or binary calculations, and specify a decisive free-energy benchmark that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing the EAM reference in TOR-TILD with a composition-specific, actively learned many-body machine-learning interatomic potential (MLIP) trained on ab initio snapshots of the target multicomponent high-entropy alloy (HEA) in both near-melting solid and liquid states will substantially increase reference–target phase-space overlap, reducing thermodynamic-integration (TI) path mismatch by roughly 3–5× in the liquid and 2–4× in the near-melting solid relative to TOR-TILD’s EAM references, and thereby lowering the free-energy bias/variance enough to predict melting free energies within ~10–20 meV/atom (or melting temperatures within ~50–100 K) of direct ab initio benchmarks.
generation.material_initial_state: Multicomponent transition-metal HEAs (4–6 components, near-equiatomic) in two phases: (i) defective near-melting crystalline solid (fcc or bcc, with thermally activated vacancies/dislocations) and (ii) homogeneous liquid, each represented by simulation cells of ≥128 atoms at ambient pressure density.
generation.intervention: Use an actively learned many-body MLIP (e.g., MTP/SNAP/GAP/NequIP-class) trained specifically on ab initio finite-T snapshots of the same HEA composition across a temperature grid bracketing the solidus and liquidus (≈0.8–1.1 Tm), then substitute this MLIP as the single reference Hamiltonian in TOR-TILD for both phases instead of EAM.
generation.conditions:
- Composition: 4–6 element transition-metal HEAs with weak-to-moderate magnetism (e.g., refractory bcc or late-transition fcc families), near-equiatomic or modest off-stoichiometry (<20 at.% deviation).
- Temperature: 0.7–1.2 Tm of the target alloy; pressures near ambient (0–1 GPa).
- Training: Active learning on ab initio MD/MC snapshots for both phases at 0.8, 0.9, 1.0, and 1.1 Tm; include chemical short-range order fluctuations and topologically diverse liquid environments; convergence targets ≤10–20 meV/atom energy MAE and ≤0.2 eV/Å force MAE on a held-out set from the same T–composition envelope.
- TI runs: NVT or NPT ensembles with ≥128–256 atoms, producing well-converged ΔU statistics at each λ; timestep and run lengths sufficient for decorrelation (e.g., ps–ns scale).
generation.structural_mediator: Accurate representation of many-body, composition-dependent local environments that govern (i) chemical short-range order and lattice anharmonicity in near-melting solids and (ii) highly heterogeneous coordination/topology in the liquid. The MLIP’s richer local descriptors capture angular/embedding physics absent in EAM, aligning the reference ensemble with the ab initio liquid/solid manifolds.
generation.mechanism: By fitting the reference Hamiltonian directly to ab initio energies/forces over the relevant high-T configuration space of the exact composition, the MLIP narrows the distribution of ΔU = U_DFT − U_ref sampled along TI. This increases reference–target phase-space overlap (lower σ[ΔU]/kT and relative entropy), reducing reweighting noise and systematic quadrature error along the λ-path. The improvement is largest in the liquid, where EAM underfits many-body and chemical-environment effects.
generation.predicted_outcome:
- Liquid (0.95–1.05 Tm): standard deviation of ΔU reduced from ~0.25–0.60 eV/atom (typical of EAM mismatch in multicomponent liquids) to ~0.05–0.12 eV/atom with the MLIP, i.e., ~3–5× reduction; corresponding drop in relative entropy D_KL by ≥70%.
- Near-melting solid (0.8–1.0 Tm): σ[ΔU] reduced from ~0.12–0.30 eV/atom (EAM) to ~0.03–0.08 eV/atom (MLIP), i.e., ~2–4× reduction.
- Practical TI impact: number of λ windows needed to achieve <1 meV/atom integration error reduced by ~2–3×; total computational effort to target the same free-energy uncertainty reduced similarly.
- Thermodynamics: resulting ab initio Gibbs free energies of solid and liquid differ by ≤10–20 meV/atom from direct DFT coexistence benchmarks, yielding melting temperatures within ~50–100 K, and demonstrably closer than EAM-referenced TOR-TILD.
generation.baseline: TOR-TILD using optimized EAM references for the same HEA compositions and state points, with identical system size, ensemble, and statistical convergence criteria.
generation.boundary:
- Alloys with strong magnetic disorder or large electronic/magnetic entropy not represented in the MLIP training (e.g., pronounced spin fluctuations) may not realize the predicted overlap gains.
- Conditions far outside the training envelope (T < 0.6 Tm or > 1.2 Tm, large compressions >5 GPa, or highly off-stoichiometric compositions) can degrade overlap.
- Long-range charge transfer or explicit electronic excitations beyond what is implicitly captured in finite-T DFT training could limit accuracy.
- Extremely small cells (<100 atoms) that cannot realize realistic liquid topology/SRO may confound the comparison.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative ranges for σ[ΔU] and free-energy improvements are extrapolated from general experience with MLIPs on elemental/binary liquids and high-T solids; specific gains for a given HEA depend on training coverage, magnetic effects, and the chosen MLIP architecture. No eligible evidence records were supplied here to anchor the numerical factors or to cite particular elemental/binary precedents; thus, the cited reduction factors (2–5×) and meV/atom targets carry moderate uncertainty and should be tested experimentally as specified below.

falsification_experiment.design: For a chosen HEA (e.g., a refractory bcc and a late-transition fcc system), construct two TOR-TILD pipelines differing only in the reference Hamiltonian: (A) best-available EAM and (B) an actively learned MLIP trained on ab initio snapshots of the same composition at 0.8, 0.9, 1.0, and 1.1 Tm, including both solid and liquid states. Use identical cells (≥128 atoms), ensembles, and convergence targets. Evaluate (i) ΔU distributions at λ=0 and selected intermediate λ, (ii) the number of λ windows required to reach <1 meV/atom quadrature error, and (iii) the resulting ab initio Gibbs free energies G_solid(T,P) and G_liquid(T,P). Independently, compute a decisive ab initio melting benchmark via a DFT two-phase coexistence simulation (or an established absolute free-energy route) to obtain Tm and G_liquid−G_solid at a fixed T near Tm.
measurements: σ[ΔU = U_DFT − U_ref] per atom for solid and liquid at 0.95–1.05 Tm (at λ=0 and along the TI path)
Relative entropy D_KL (or equivalent overlap metric) between reference and DFT ensembles for both phases
Number of λ windows needed to achieve <1 meV/atom TI integration error
Ab initio free-energy difference ΔG = G_liquid − G_solid at a reference T near Tm
Melting temperature Tm from DFT two-phase coexistence (or equivalent absolute free-energy crossing)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if any of the following hold for the liquid near Tm: (1) σ[ΔU] reduction using MLIP vs EAM is <50% (i.e., <2× improvement), or D_KL reduction is <70%; (2) the number of λ windows to reach <1 meV/atom error is not reduced by at least 2×; or (3) the MLIP-referenced TOR-TILD free energy differs from the decisive DFT benchmark by >20 meV/atom (or the corresponding Tm deviates by >100 K), and does not improve over the EAM-referenced result.
